title: Process Injection: Portable Executable Injection
summary: This sub-technique covers placing an executable image directly into the memory of another live process rather than loading a library by name. A portable executable is the standard Windows program format, and the injector copies that image, which may never exist as a file on the target disk, into memory reserved inside the victim process, then transfers control to it through a newly created thread or a small stub of position independent code. The awkward part for the attacker is relocation: the image was not mapped by the loader, so addresses baked into it do not match where it now sits, and the payload must be written so that this can be corrected at runtime, which is a useful distinguishing feature because it tends to produce unusual memory protections and self modifying code. Defensively this looks like memory that is both writable and executable and that no mapped file backs, plus a thread whose start address falls outside any known module. Legitimate software rarely creates such pages, though some runtimes and packers do, so a finding should be confirmed against the module list of that process before it is treated as hostile.

beginner.definition: A portable executable is the file format Windows uses for programs. This sub-technique is when an attacker writes a whole program straight into the memory of another running program. It is part of the Process Injection parent technique. The difference is that no reusable library file is involved.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because the code is copied rather than loaded as a file, disk scanning may find nothing at all. The activity appears under the name of a normal process, so simple allow lists can be fooled. The copied program needs fixing up as it runs, which leaves unusual signs that a careful defender can use. Learning those signs helps you find what file checks miss.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a target process and obtains the right to work inside its memory.
They reserve writable space in that process, large enough to hold their copied program.
They write the program image into the new space, but the addresses inside it are now wrong.
They add code that repairs those addresses at run time, so the program can execute where it sits.
They start a thread in the target process to run the copied code, or jump to it from existing code.
The result is active code in a familiar process with no matching program file on the disk.
beginner.example: Think of a courier depot where every box arrives with a printed label showing its shelf. Someone unpacks a parcel in the loading bay and rebuilds it on a different shelf. Then they rewrite the label by hand to match the new position. The depot system has no record of the parcel at all. Staff walk past it all day, because it sits among legitimate boxes. Only an inspector who checks labels against the register sees the odd one.
takeaways: Code can run with no program file present on the disk.
Writable and executable memory with no backing file is a key warning sign.
A thread starting outside any known module deserves investigation.

objectives: Explain what a portable executable is and how this differs from loading a library by name.
Describe why copied code needs address correction and how that leaves artefacts.
Identify the memory protection and thread evidence produced by this injection.
Explain how this technique defeats file based scanning and signature checks.
Compare suspicious executable memory with legitimate cases such as runtimes and packers.
